query: Prior calculations on concentrated alloys examined variations in atomic mass and force constants, temperature-dependent lattice heat transport, or DFT-derived elastic properties coupled to analytical conductivity estimates; some estimates require a Debye temperature. The cited simulations generally represented perfect, defect-free bulk crystals. Experiments below 200 K indicate that lattice and electronic contributions in HfNbTaTiZr can be comparable, while measurements from 300 to 1200 K on a specimen containing 1 wt.% oxygen report total conductivity of 10–17 W/(K m). Available analytical approaches do not capture all relevant atomic-scale complexity in refractory high-entropy alloys, and separate transport studies do not establish a predictive solution for this alloy. Given these constraints, what testable hypothesis could an unspecified new predictive approach make for HfNbTaTiZr without conflating lattice and electronic heat transport? Explain why it should outperform earlier approaches, quantify the expected improvement, define its temperature and sample applicability limits, identify supporting observations from the cited work, and specify decisive comparisons with low- and high-temperature measurements that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: A new predictive approach that decouples lattice and electronic heat transport—by combining high-fidelity DFT calculations with machine‐learning models that explicitly capture the effects of atomic mass and force constant disorder—will predict the lattice thermal conductivity of defect‐free HfNbTaTiZr with roughly 20–30% improved accuracy compared to earlier models that use Debye temperature and averaged elastic properties. Moreover, the approach will separately resolve the lattice and electronic contributions below 200 K where they are comparable.
generation.intervention: Apply the new predictive approach that integrates refined DFT, on-the-fly machine learning, and an analytical treatment of force constant and mass fluctuations
generation.conditions: Measurements should be conducted over a wide temperature range—from below 200 K (to capture comparable lattice and electronic conduction) up to 1200 K on samples with minimal oxygen contamination (<1 wt.%)—to ensure that the effects of atomic-scale disorder are isolated from extrinsic defects.
generation.structural_mediator: Atomic-scale mass and force constant disorder (i.e., chemical short-range order) that mediates phonon scattering
generation.mechanism: By modeling the scattering of phonons in a chemically disordered and defect-free lattice separately from electronic contributions, the approach leverages the explicit treatment of force constant fluctuations to predict the lattice component more accurately. This mechanism should result in temperature-dependent trends that distinctly separate the lattice and electronic thermal conductivities, especially evident at low temperatures.
generation.predicted_outcome: The method will yield lattice thermal conductivity predictions that align with experimental measurements within a 20–30% margin of error over 300–1200 K. In the low temperature regime (<200 K), the model will predict two distinct trends—one for lattice and one for electronic contributions—where earlier approaches, which conflated the two, would fail to capture the separation.
generation.baseline: Earlier approaches based on Debye temperature estimates and DFT-derived elastic properties combined with analytical conductivity approximations that do not separately resolve lattice and electronic contributions
generation.boundary: The predictive improvement is expected for nearly ideal, defect‐free, and minimally oxygen-contaminated HfNbTaTiZr samples; its validity may diminish in samples with significant extrinsic defects or impurities. The most robust prediction is anticipated in the temperature range of 300–1200 K, with increased uncertainty below 200 K due to the close interplay of lattice and electronic transport.
generation.uncertainty: The estimated 20–30% improvement is based on the anticipated efficacy of decoupling mechanisms under ideal conditions; actual improvements may vary with sample quality and unaccounted nano-scale heterogeneities.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of defect-free HfNbTaTiZr samples with oxygen content strictly controlled below 1 wt.%. Measure total thermal conductivity from cryogenic temperatures (below 200 K) up to 1200 K using independent techniques capable of deconvoluting lattice and electronic contributions (e.g., using terahertz spectroscopy for electronic components). Then, apply the new predictive model to obtain separate predictions for the lattice and electronic conductivities at these temperatures.
measurements: Independent measurements of lattice thermal conductivity over 300–1200 K
Measurements of electronic conductivity and its thermal contribution at temperatures below 200 K
Comparison of total versus separated contributions as predicted by the model
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the new predictive approach does not achieve at least a 20% improvement in accuracy (relative to the baseline models) for the lattice thermal conductivity across the 300–1200 K range, or if it fails to distinctly resolve the lattice and electronic contributions at temperatures below 200 K—leading to overlapping or conflated trends—the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
Phonon behavior in a random solid solution: a lattice dynamics study on the high-entropy alloy FeCoCrMnNi

Abstract: AbstractHigh-Entropy Alloys (HEAs) are a new family of crystalline random alloys with four or more elements in a simple unit cell, at the forefront of materials research for their exceptional mechanical properties. Their strong chemical disorder leads to mass and force-constant fluctuations which are expected to strongly reduce phonon lifetime, responsible for thermal transport, similarly to glasses. Still, the long range order would associate HEAs to crystals with a complex disordered unit cell. These two families of materials, however, exhibit very different phonon dynamics, still leading to similar thermal properties. The question arises on the positioning of HEAs in this context. Here we present an exhaustive experimental investigation of the lattice dynamics in a HEA, Fe20Co20Cr20Mn20Ni20, using inelastic neutron and X-ray scattering. We demonstrate that HEAs present unique phonon dynamics at the frontier between fully disordered and ordered materials, characterized by long-propagating acoustic phonons in the whole Brillouin zone.Subject terms: Electronic proper
